answers.answer: Fifty boxes of earth. They were delivered to the ruined chapel of the Carfax house, near Purfleet (e0071.1, e0155.2). Some were later removed: a carter's account (e0171.4, e0171.3) says nine went to the house in Piccadilly (five on the first load, four on the second). The passages I read do not give a final count of how many were left at Carfax.

First mentioned on 26 July 1893 by Mina, in her journal: Lucy 'has lately taken to her old habit of walking in her sleep', and Mina and Mrs. Westenra decide Mina will lock their door each night (e0044.1). The phrase 'old habit' implies earlier episodes that the store does not record.

Only one of Lucy's entries never mentions Arthur: her diary entry of 12 September 1893 (e0106.1), which talks about the garlic and sleep. The other eight entries (two letters to Mina, and her diary and memorandum entries) all name Arthur.

Four transfusions, in order: Arthur Holmwood (7 September, e0100.6 and e0100.8; Van Helsing said 'John was to give his blood' but Arthur was present and gave it), then Dr. Seward (10 September, e0104.2), then Van Helsing himself (13 September, e0107.4 with e0127.2 'I give my blood for her'), then Quincey Morris (18 September, e0116.6 and e0116.7, 'A brave man's blood is the best thing on this earth').

The garlic came from Haarlem, from the glass-houses of Van Helsing's friend Vanderpool, who grew it all year; Van Helsing had telegraphed for it (e0105.2). Van Helsing arranged the flowers in the room with Seward's help (e0105.2, e0124.4), and Lucy also received a boxful daily from Haarlem (e0108.1).

'Vampire' first appears on 5 May 1893, in Jonathan Harker's journal at the Castle, where he records that the Slovak and Servian travellers spoke of something 'either were-wolf or vampire' (e0004.1). It is the earliest match in the store's date-ordered grep.

One document: a letter dated 25 May 1893 from Quincey P. Morris to Hon. Arthur Holmwood, signed 'QUINCEY P. MORRIS'. It invites Arthur to a camp-fire the next night, with Jack Seward also coming (e0030.1). Morris's other appearances in the records are in other people's entries, and the store shows no other document in his own hand.

experience: The task-start warnings were the most useful part. DECOMPOSITION_REQUIRED and the COUNT and NEGATION warnings pointed me to exact tools: grep for the transfusion and garlic terms, and list --by-entry for the Lucy-without-Arthur complement. SUPERLATIVE and its date-order advice made the sleepwalking and vampire questions quick. Semantic search was less useful on its own: the Q1 search for boxes returned off-topic Harker passages (OFF_QUESTION fired on e0161.5 and e0154.1), and most of its top results were not about the question. The truncated excerpts (about 200 words, 'part 2/10') meant I often had to read a neighbouring part, and I could not tell from the excerpt whether an entry continued. The read on a guessed id, e0107.5, crashed with a Python KeyError traceback and no message the tool could use. Grepping 'Art' for Arthur was ambiguous, since it also catches 'Art' as a nickname in Morris's letter. I wish the output said how many boxes were recorded as removed in total, and whether a count stated in one record was contradicted by another. I also wish list --by-entry showed the matching passage text, so I could check the hit without a second read.
